question: Nina covers four cells of a 3 by 3 grid with square tiles: A1, B1, C1 and C2. Rows are A to C from the top, columns 1 to 3 from the left. Each tile has sides of 1 cm. What is the perimeter of her shape in centimetres?
hint: Walk around the shape and count every tile side on the outside.
solution: Four tiles have 16 sides in all. Three pairs of tiles touch, and each touching pair hides 2 sides. 16 - 6 = 10 cm.

A.text: 8 misses the two sides in the inner corner of the shape.

B.text: 16 also counts the sides where two tiles touch, which are inside.

D.text: 4 is how many tiles there are, the area, not the way round.

E.text: 5 is only the height plus the width; go all the way round.

question: A mosaic is a square of 3 by 3 tiles, each 1 cm by 1 cm. The artist takes away the four corner tiles. What area do the tiles that are left cover, in square centimetres?
hint: How many tiles were there before any were taken away?
solution: The square has 3 × 3 = 9 tiles. Taking away 4 corners leaves 9 - 4 = 5 tiles, so they cover 5 square centimetres.

A.text: 9 is the whole square before the corners go.

B.text: 4 is the number of tiles the artist took away.

C.text: 12 is the length around the shape, its perimeter.

E.text: 6 counts the centre tile twice, once in each line.

question: A garden is a 4 by 4 grid of square beds, with rows A to D and columns 1 to 4. Roses grow in beds B2, B3, C2 and C3. How many other beds share a whole side with a rose bed?
hint: Look at each side of the rose square: which beds touch it there?
solution: Two beds touch each of the four sides of the rose square: A2 and A3 above, D2 and D3 below, B1 and C1 on the left, B4 and C4 on the right. That makes 8 beds.

A.text: 6 leaves out the two beds along one side.

C.text: 12 adds the corner beds, which only touch at a point.

D.text: 4 is the number of rose beds themselves.

E.text: 16 gives every rose bed four neighbours, rose beds among them.

question: A playground is marked on a grid of squares with sides of 1 m. It takes up seven squares: A1, B1, C1, C2, C3, B3 and A3, where A to C are the rows from the top. How many metres of fence go all the way round it?
hint: Does the fence also have to run down into the gap in the middle?
solution: Seven squares have 28 sides. Six pairs of squares touch, and each pair hides 2 sides. 28 - 12 = 16 metres of fence.

A.text: 12 fences the whole 3 by 3 square, not this shape.

B.text: 15 misses the piece of fence along the bottom of the gap.

C.text: 7 is how many squares it takes up, its area.

D.text: 28 counts the sides where squares touch each other.

question: In a board game, a domino covers two squares of a 3 by 3 board that share a side. Rows are A to C from the top, columns 1 to 3 from the left. Two placements are different if they cover different squares. In how many ways can the domino be placed?
hint: Count the places for a domino lying across first, then for one standing up.
solution: Lying across, each row has 2 places, so 3 rows give 6. Standing up, each column has 2 places, so 3 columns give 6. In all, 6 + 6 = 12 ways.

B.text: 24 counts each placement once from each of its two squares.

C.text: 9 is the number of squares on the board.

D.text: 6 forgets the dominoes that stand up.

E.text: 18 lets a domino stick out over the edge of the board.

question: A square cake is cut into 3 by 3 equal square pieces with sides of 2 cm. Rows are A to C from the top, columns 1 to 3 from the left. Oleg eats one corner piece. What is the perimeter of the cake that is left, in centimetres?
hint: Which sides of the cake does the eaten piece take away, and which new sides appear?
solution: The whole cake is 6 cm long on each side, so its perimeter is 4 × 6 = 24 cm. The eaten piece takes away two outer sides of 2 cm, and two of its inner sides of 2 cm become outer instead. The perimeter stays 24 cm.

A.text: 22 takes one side of the piece away from 24.

C.text: 20 takes away the two lost sides but forgets the two new ones.

D.text: 28 adds the two new sides but keeps the two lost ones.

E.text: 32 square centimetres is the area of the cake left.

question: A chocolate bar has 2 rows of 3 squares. Rows are A and B from the top, columns 1 to 3 from the left. Kim and Lev break it along the lines into two pieces of 3 squares each, and each piece must hold together by whole sides. Two ways are different if they split the squares differently. How many ways are there?
hint: After the straight break, look for pieces shaped like a corner.
solution: A straight break gives the two rows of 3. A corner-shaped piece works too: the left column with the next top square, or the left column with the next bottom square, and the other 3 squares hold together each time. That makes 3 ways.

A.text: 7 includes splits where the second piece falls apart.

B.text: 2 misses one of the two corner-shaped splits.

C.text: 1 stops at the straight break; corner pieces work too.

E.text: 6 counts each split twice, once for each piece.

question: A square pond fills the middle of a 3 by 3 grid, and the other 8 squares are paving slabs. Rows are A to C from the top, columns 1 to 3 from the left. Two gardeners share the slabs, 4 each, and each gardener's slabs have to stay joined by whole sides. Splits count as different when the groups of slabs are different. How many splits are possible?
hint: The slabs make a ring around the pond. What must a group of 4 joined slabs look like?
solution: The 8 slabs form a ring, so 4 slabs that stay joined are 4 in a row around it, and so are the other 4. The ring has 8 such runs of 4, and each split uses two of them: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 splits.

B.text: 8 counts each split twice, once for each gardener.

C.text: 28 cuts the ring in any two places and forgets the 4 each.

D.text: 1 stops after the first split; turn it around the ring.

E.text: 2 finds the splits across the rows but not across the columns.

question: Pasha lays 4 square tiles with sides of 1 cm on a table to make one shape, each tile touching another along a whole side. What is the largest perimeter the shape can have, in centimetres?
hint: Each time two tiles share a side, how much of the perimeter disappears?
solution: Four tiles have 16 cm of sides. Each shared side hides 2 cm. One shape of 4 tiles needs at least 3 shared sides, so the most is 16 - 6 = 10 cm, as a straight line of 4 tiles has.

A.text: 16 counts the sides where tiles touch each other.

B.text: 8 is the smallest perimeter, the 2 by 2 square.

D.text: 12 is two pairs lying apart, not one shape.

E.text: 4 is the area in square centimetres.
